JSON: Name: llm_w2rkg_pipeline Title: Automated construction of waste-to-resource knowledge graphs for industrial symbiosis identification using an LLM-based retrieval, event-argument extraction, and fusion pipeline Short Hypothesis: Applying an LLM-based pipeline composed of retrieval, event-argument extraction, and fusion to research-paper corpora produces a waste-to-resource knowledge graph with significantly higher recall of valid W2R relationships than a sequential NER+RE baseline while maintaining micro-F1 ≥ 0.80 on extraction tasks. Related Work: Existing work on waste-to-resource (W2R) knowledge has relied primarily on manual curation of case-based databases and on conventional NLP pipelines. Manually built W2R resources provide high-precision, validated case records but scale poorly and cover a limited range of potential W2R pathways. Conventional automated approaches adopt modular NER+relation-extraction or embedding-based matching to link materials, but they suffer from low coverage (miss unimplemented or literature-only pathways), brittle relation modelling for process-like relationships, and limited standardization (duplicates, heterogeneous naming). Recent efforts attempt partial automation using embeddings to link materials and lightweight extraction, but they encounter an encoding bottleneck and positional/context limits for long scientific texts. Large language models (LLMs) have been demonstrated for various KGC subtasks (zero-/few-shot extraction, canonicalization, code-style structured outputs) and can reduce annotation needs, but prior LLM applications either focus on single subtasks, generate unparsable outputs, or scale poorly to document-level retrieval and canonicalization. Open problems remain in: (1) combining document retrieval with LLM extraction to avoid context loss, (2) framing W2R extraction as event-argument extraction to better capture process-like relations, (3) robust canonicalization and fusion at scale (clustering + LLM canonicalization), and (4) rigorous, reproducible evaluation of coverage versus precision trade-offs against curated databases. Abstract: We propose an end-to-end research pipeline that uses large language models to automatically construct a waste-to-resource knowledge graph (W2RKG) from research literature to support industrial symbiosis identification. The pipeline integrates four modules: data preparation and document retrieval to select W2R-relevant text chunks, event-argument extraction (waste, transforming process, transformed resource) using LLM prompting (JSON/code styles), and a two-stage fusion module that clusters entities (HAC) and canonicalizes representations with LLM-assisted matching. The primary contribution is a validated, parameterized pipeline demonstrating that LLM-enabled extraction plus systematic fusion increases W2R coverage compared to manual databases while retaining high extraction quality. Expected outcomes include (1) a reproducible procedure for large-scale W2RKG construction from academic corpora, (2) quantitative evaluation of prompting styles, retrieval granularity, model choices (open vs. closed LLMs), and fusion thresholds, and (3) an assessed W2RKG suitable for downstream company-to-company matching. The pipeline is intended to provide a scalable, standardised W2R knowledge resource for industrial symbiosis planning and discovery. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Corpus: 4,499 research-paper records retrieved from Scopus with search tokens related to waste-to-resource and waste valorization published after 2017; include full texts where available (77 review papers) and abstracts for all papers. (2) Annotated extraction set: 150 manually annotated abstracts (100 for model development/fine-tuning, 50 held-out for evaluation). (3) Coverage benchmark: MAESTRI W2R database (425 records) and a curated set of 100 randomly sampled W2R relationships from MAESTRI for manual matching evaluation. (4) Final KG sampling: random sample N=100 W2R relationships extracted from the constructed KG for manual alignment/validness evaluation by three annotators. Baselines: (A) rule-based pipeline: rule-based NER + pattern RE (regex + dependency rules); (B) sequential ML pipeline: fine-tuned NER (BiLSTM-CRF or BERT) + supervised RE classifier; (C) embedding-only linking: embedding cosine similarity linking without LLM extraction; (D) open-source LLaMa3.1 fine-tuned EAE (LoRA) ablation. Models/Variants to compare: GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, LLaMa3.1 (pretrained, few-shot, and LoRA fine-tuned), JSON-style prompting vs code-style prompting, zero-shot vs 2-shot vs 10-shot where applicable. Retrieval ablations: chunk size 500/1000/2000 chars and overlap 100/200; with vs without retrieval module. Fusion ablations: HAC distance thresholds {0.1,0.2,0.4}; canonicalization by LLM (GPT-4o-mini) vs embedding nearest-neighbor. Evaluation metrics: micro-precision, micro-recall, micro-F1 on extraction (waste, resource; transforming process optional), Jaccard similarity for set-level matches, alignment and validness rates (binary majority-vote scores) on sampled KG, coverage fraction of MAESTRI relationships recovered, Cohen's kappa for annotator agreement, and statistical significance via paired bootstrap (95% CI). Experimental setup: LoRA fine-tuning on LLaMa3.1-8B using 4-bit quantization on a T4 (16GB) GPU; token limit 2048 for fine-tuning; LLM API calls logged and cost recorded. Prompting experiments run with three random seeds; report mean ± std. Ablation studies: (1) extraction prompt style (JSON vs code), (2) shot count (0/2/10), (3) retrieval on/off, (4) fusion threshold sweep, (5) canonicalization method. Success criteria: pipeline achieves micro-F1 ≥ 0.80 on held-out annotated extraction set and recovers ≥ 50% of MAESTRI W2R relationships while increasing total unique W2R pairs by ≥ 5x relative to MAESTRI. Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) LLM hallucination and unparsable outputs: LLM-generated structured outputs can be syntactically invalid or contain invented entities and relations; such failures reduce precision and complicate automated parsing. 2) Retrieval and context limits: long documents and limited context windows can cause omission of dispersed W2R evidence; retrieval chunking parameters critically affect recall and introduce positional bias. 3) Annotation and evaluation noise: ground-truth databases (e.g., MAESTRI) and manual annotations contain errors or inconsistent granularity, complicating coverage measurements and metric interpretation. 4) Canonicalization brittleness: clustering distance thresholds and embedding/canonicalization choices can conflate distinct concepts or split identical concepts, affecting graph quality. 5) Cost and scalability: reliance on proprietary LLM APIs (e.g., GPT-4o) incurs substantial cost for large corpora; local fine-tuning of large models requires multi-GPU resources. 6) Domain and data bias: limiting sources to academic literature omits industrial reports and patents, biasing the KG toward research topics and underrepresenting operational constraints (quantities, purity, regulatory factors). 7) Limited process modelling: representing transforming processes as relationship properties rather than full process nodes omits concurrency and multi-waste-to-single-resource semantics. 8) Legal/copyright constraints: full-text usage and redistribution are limited by publisher copyrights, restricting data sharing and reproducibility for some artifacts. 9) Generalization limits: models and prompts tuned on English scientific abstracts may perform poorly on other languages or domain subfields with different terminology.
